title: Gas fire in the kitchen
summary: Flames appear around an LPG cylinder's regulator while the stove is on. Get everyone safe.
sources: National Disaster Management Authority (India): fire safety guidance
Indian Oil / Bharat Gas / HP Gas LPG consumer safety advice

scenes.narration: You're making tea. There's a strong smell of gas, then a hiss, and small flames flicker around the cylinder's regulator under the counter.

choices.label: Stop: there's a gas fire at the cylinder
choices.feedback: Right. A smell of gas plus flames at the cylinder is an emergency. Recognising it fast buys you time.

choices.label: It's probably just the burner. Keep cooking.
choices.feedback: Flames at the regulator are not the burner. Fires around gas cylinders can grow very quickly.

scenes.narration: The flames are growing around the cylinder. Your little brother is watching TV in the next room, and your grandmother is upstairs.

choices.label: Others are in danger: everyone must get out
choices.feedback: Yes. People come first. The fire is near a gas cylinder, which you must not approach.

choices.label: It's small. I can handle it myself.
choices.feedback: A fire at a gas cylinder is not a beginner's fire. Approaching it puts you at serious risk.

choices.label: Switch on the kitchen light and fan to see better
choices.feedback: Never operate electrical switches when there is gas in the air: a switch can spark and ignite it.

scenes.narration: Smoke is gathering at the ceiling. What do you do now?

choices.label: Shout "Fire! Get out!" and lead everyone outside, closing doors behind you
choices.feedback: Exactly. Alert, get out and close doors to slow the fire and smoke.

choices.label: Go to the cylinder and try to turn off the regulator
choices.feedback: Do not approach a burning cylinder. Get out and let the fire service deal with it.

choices.label: Throw a bucket of water on the flames
choices.feedback: Water does not stop burning gas, and you'd have to get close. Leave it to firefighters.

choices.label: Stay in the kitchen and call 112
choices.feedback: Calling is right, but do it from a safe place outside. Get everyone out first.

scenes.narration: Everyone is out on the street. Smoke is coming from the kitchen window.

choices.label: Call 112 and give the full address and what's burning
choices.feedback: Right. Tell them it's an LPG cylinder fire so the fire service comes prepared. Warn the neighbours too.

choices.label: Run back in to grab your phone and valuables
choices.feedback: Never go back into a burning building. Things can be replaced; people cannot.

choices.label: Wait and see if it burns itself out
choices.feedback: Fires near gas cylinders can get worse suddenly. Call for help straight away.

end-safe.text: Firefighters arrive and put out the fire. Everyone is safe because you got out early and called for help.

end-unsafe.text: Going back inside exposed you to heavy smoke. Firefighters bring you out coughing. In real life this is how people get hurt.

learn: Smell of gas or flames at a cylinder: get everyone out and call 112 from outside.
Never operate switches, lighters or phones near leaking gas: sparks can ignite it.
Do not approach a burning cylinder or try to fight the fire yourself.
Close doors behind you to slow fire and smoke, and never go back inside.
disclaimer: Training only. This is not a substitute for emergency services or certified first-aid and fire-safety training. In a real emergency in India, call 112.
